name: Today's Report
headline: Same number of sellers, slower sales: the Tri-City inventory build is a drain story, not a supply story.
teaser: Mortgage rates finished the week almost exactly where they started. Mortgage News Daily had the 30-year at 7.20% and the 15-year at 6.83% as of Friday, September 18, and nothing reprices over a weekend. The 10-Year Treasury closed Friday at 5.01%, which is the highest a 10-Year has been since July 2007.

sections.label: Real estate
sections.html:
Mortgage rates finished the week almost exactly where they started. Mortgage News Daily had the 30-year at 7.20% and the 15-year at 6.83% as of Friday, September 18, and nothing reprices over a weekend. The 10-Year Treasury closed Friday at 5.01%, which is the highest a 10-Year has been since July 2007.

Today we want to spend the space on something more useful than a rate that did not move. Harv pulled twenty months of inventory for Fremont, Newark and Union City, and the three cities are not telling the same story.

Start with the floor rather than the peak. Every year inventory drains through the winter and rebuilds through the spring, so the summer peak is the number everyone quotes and the January trough is the number that actually tells you what carried over. Fremont started 2025 with 150 homes for sale and started 2026 with 216, a 44% higher floor. Newark went from 50 to 57. Union City went from 51 to 50, which is to say it did not build at all.

Now the part that surprised us. Across the three cities, 1,699 new listings came to market from January through August this year against 1,708 over the same eight months last year, a difference of half a percent. The faucet is running at the same rate it always was. What changed is how fast the tub drains.

  • What that means in practice: the extra inventory you are seeing in Fremont is not a wave of new sellers. It is the same number of sellers, with their homes staying on the market longer.
  • Why Union City looks different: it is the one city of the three that cleared what arrived. Today its typical listing has been out 24 days against Fremont's 30.

Alameda County (Fremont Focus)

  • Board wide: 2,768 listings across our 15 city table, counting active and in contract together, with 190 coming soon and 237 brand new.
  • Five city ledger: 716 live listings across Fremont, Hayward, Milpitas, Newark and Union City. 632 are already on the market and 84 are coming soon.
  • Fremont: 255 live, 201 active, 36 coming soon, 18 brand new. The median on market list price is $1,200,000 at $794 a square foot, and the typical active listing has been out 30 days.
  • Newark: 91 live, 79 on the market, median $1,198,000 at $685 a square foot, typical listing out 24 days, and only 12 homes sitting 60 days or longer.
  • Union City: 68 live, 61 on the market, median $1,250,000 at $767 a square foot, typical listing out 24 days. The highest median of the three, on the smallest inventory.
  • The rest of the ledger: Hayward 187, Milpitas 115.
  • Across all five cities the median is $1,099,000 at $682 a square foot. 283 homes are priced under a million, and 161 have been sitting 60 days or longer.
  • The local math: at Fremont's median list price of $1,200,000, a 20% down loan is $960,000, under Alameda County's $1,249,125 high-balance conforming limit.
  • At 7.20%, principal and interest run about $6,516 a month, and every eighth of a point is about $81.

What this means for you: if you are listing in Fremont this fall you are not competing with more sellers, you are competing with sellers who have already been out there a while and are getting tired. That is a pricing conversation, not a timing one. In Newark and Union City the standing inventory is genuinely thinner, so a well priced home still gets its weekend. Sellers: price to the 7.2% a buyer is actually quoted, not to the rate anybody hoped for in June.

images.alt: Two panel line chart of homes for sale each month from January 2025 through August 2026. Fremont rises from 150 in January 2025 to a 216 floor in January 2026 while its summer peak moves only from 386 to 398. Newark rises from 50 to 57 and Union City is flat at 51 then 50.
images.caption: Fremont started 2026 with 44% more homes on the market than it started 2025, while its summer peak barely moved. Newark built a smaller floor. Union City built none at all.
images.source: Source: Zillow Research, for-sale inventory, smoothed, single family and condo, monthly through August 2026. Not the same basis as the MLS board counts above.

images.alt: Bar and line chart for Fremont, Newark and Union City combined, January 2025 through August 2026. Bars show new listings arriving each month, running at nearly identical levels in both years. The line shows homes standing for sale, which runs higher throughout 2026, peaking at 626 against 592 in 2025.
images.caption: 1,699 new listings arrived from January through August this year against 1,708 last year, a difference of half a percent. The standing inventory is higher anyway, which means homes are leaving more slowly than they arrive.
images.source: Source: Zillow Research, for-sale inventory and new listings, both smoothed, single family and condo, monthly through August 2026. Two different units, so both axes start at zero and only the shapes are comparable.

sections.label: Economy
sections.html:
The 10-Year Treasury closed Friday at 5.01%. That is the highest close since July 19, 2007, which we checked against the Treasury's own daily yield curve rather than taking a newsletter's word for it. It is also the single most important number in this report, because the 30-year mortgage is priced off it.

Market Briefs built its Sunday edition around the dollar losing value, and the argument holds up better than some of its numbers. Two corrections. It put gold "near $4,350"; gold actually settled Friday at $4,424.90. And its "record near $5,600 in January" is an intraday tick from January 29, not a close. Gold's record close is $5,318.40 from the same day, which is still a long way above where it sits now.

Oil did the real moving. Brent settled Friday at $99.29, down 5.28% on the day, and back under $100 for the first time since early September. Gold and silver both went the other way, with silver up 2.19% to $67.15.

Silver is worth a second look for anyone who has been watching gold. It has now outrun gold over the past week, and unlike gold it has an industrial floor under it.

sections.label: Stocks
sections.html:
All three indexes finished Friday within a quarter percent of flat, which is about as quiet as a week ends. The Nasdaq was the only one with a real gain at +0.39%, the Dow the only loss at -0.18%.

These are the same closes we printed yesterday, because Saturday and Sunday do not produce new ones. The next real print is Monday's open.

sections.label: Crypto
sections.html:
Crypto is the one section that actually moves on a Sunday, and it moved down. All three of ours are off slightly over the past 24 hours, with XRP the weakest at -1.38%.

Quotes are live as of this morning with 24 hour changes, so unlike the stock and metals numbers above these are genuinely today's.
